paras: The threatened lynching of Ore Brown took place in Madison, Wisconsin, on July 2, 1903, when railroad men threatened to lynch Brown, a young Black man accused of attempting to assault two little girls near the State Capitol. Police captured and guarded him, no mob formed, and he later pleaded guilty and was sentenced to six years in state prison. The New-York Tribune presented the episode as a lynching prevented by prompt police action, while a wire version circulated in Midwestern papers under headlines about lynching talk and a "foul crime."

According to the wire report, Brown was 20 years old and had served a year for burglary, having been released six months earlier. The reports give the accusers' ages differently: the Tribune said the girls were five and seven, while the wire said both were eight and described them as white.

On the afternoon of July 2, Brown was accused of attempting to assault the two girls under a railroad bridge about half a dozen blocks from the statehouse. Their screams brought help, and Brown got away, by bicycle according to the wire, before police captured him later that day.

The Tribune's correspondent reported that a detail of officers was hurried to protect Brown from railroad men who threatened to lynch him. Brown was taken to the city prison, and that night police prevented any number of people from gathering anywhere in the city, especially near the jail. Officials conferred with the Governor but decided not to call out troops unless a mob formed. The wire account described only "some talk of lynching" when news of the assault first spread and said the authorities did not fear trouble.

In mid-August a Wisconsin state-news column reported that "Ora Brown," the man accused of the attempted assault on two little girls at Madison, had pleaded guilty and been sentenced to six years in state prison. No report of any action against those who threatened him appears in the coverage.

The New-York Tribune ran its own telegraphed report on July 3 under the headline "Prevent Lynching in Wisconsin," with the subhead "Police Protect from Railroad Men Negro Accused by Two Little Girls." The same day the Minneapolis Journal printed a fuller wire version headed "Talked of Lynching," which stated the assault as fact rather than as an accusation. A shortened form of that wire story reached South Dakota and North Dakota weeklies on July 9 and 10 under the headline "Negroe's Foul Crime" and the subhead "Indignant People Talk of Lynching the Beast."
The sentence was noted in brief in Wisconsin state-news columns in the Wausau Pilot and the Vernon County Censor on August 18 and 19. No coverage of the episode in the Black press was found.

The two July reports differ on the girls' ages, five and seven in the Tribune against eight in the wire, and on how serious the lynching threat was. The Tribune described named threats from railroad men, a police guard and a conference with the Governor, while the wire mentioned only passing talk of lynching that the authorities did not fear.

bases: Brown was threatened with lynching after his arrest, but police guarded him and no mob formed or attacked (A1, A2).
Nobody was killed: railroad men threatened to lynch Brown and there was 'talk of lynching' over an alleged assault, but police held him and he was later sentenced in court (A1, A2, A6).

accounts.label: Tribune special telegraph
accounts.gist: Police acted promptly to prevent a lynching, guarding Brown from railroad men who threatened to lynch him and dispersing any gathering; the Governor was consulted about troops.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Brown assaulted two eight-year-old white girls but was driven off; he fled on a bicycle, was caught, and there was 'some talk of lynching' that the authorities no longer feared.

accounts.label: Wisconsin state-news column
accounts.gist: Brown pleaded guilty to attempted assault and received six years in state prison.

framing.detail: The Tribune's headline 'Prevent Lynching in Wisconsin' centres the police action and calls Brown a 'Negro Accused by Two Little Girls'.
The wire story states the assault as fact; the Minneapolis Journal headed it 'Talked of Lynching', while Dakota weeklies ran it as 'Negroe's Foul Crime' with the subhead 'Lynching the Beast'.

conflicts.note: The two reports appear to come from different sources (special telegraph vs. wire); neither is clearly better.

info: Accusation, capture and lynching threats on the afternoon and night of July 2, 1903 (Tribune dateline July 2 'to-night'; wire, filed July 3, says 'yesterday afternoon')
Madison, Wisconsin, within five blocks of the Capitol; the wire places the alleged assault under a railroad bridge about half a dozen blocks from the statehouse
Ore Brown (also 'Ora Brown'), a young Black man ('negro'), aged 20 per the wire
Accused of attempting to criminally assault two little white girls (ages given as five and seven, or both eight)
Railroad men who threatened to lynch him (Tribune); 'indignant people' and 'some talk of lynching' (wire)
Brown pleaded guilty to attempted assault on two little girls and was sentenced to six years in state prison
